title: Growth: which engine is accelerating, and why GDP won't tell you
hook:
On a Friday morning in September 2019, Nirmala Sitharaman walked into a press conference in Goa and announced one of the biggest corporate tax cuts in India's history. The Sensex had its best day in over a decade. Cement makers, banks and carmakers rocketed. Commentators predicted a new wave of factory building.

Here's the twist. Company profits did jump, because companies were simply paying less tax. But the great private investment boom took years to arrive, and when it finally did, it came only in the handful of industries where the government was paying people to build. The rest of corporate India pocketed the savings and waited.

That gap between what the headline promised and what actually happened is the subject of this chapter. India's growth is not one number. It is several engines running at different speeds, and stock returns follow whichever engine is speeding up. So which one is it right now?
short: Headline GDP growth is the least useful growth number for equities. Sector returns follow whichever part of demand is accelerating, and in this cycle the parts have moved far apart.
Public capex carried the post-pandemic recovery. Private investment followed only where incentives point: electronics, power equipment and transmission, renewables and defence.
Consumption is split in two: premium and urban-affluent demand has held up while mass and rural demand lagged. The 2025 tax and GST cuts targeted the mass segment; fuel and rates now work against it.
Services exports steady the external account but have slowed; goods exports face US tariffs, with electronics the incentive-driven exception.
The capex engine still has momentum but is decelerating from a very high pace. Expect dispersion inside the index to widen.

sections.heading: Why GDP is the wrong growth number for your portfolio
sections.html:
GDP is a sum. It adds up what households spend, what companies and the government invest, what the government spends on running itself, and what India sells abroad minus what it buys. Every quarter the headline number lands, TV anchors debate whether it was good or bad, and the stock market mostly shrugs.

Why the shrug? Three reasons. First, the stock market is not the economy. Farming and small informal businesses are a big chunk of GDP and barely exist on the exchange, while banks, IT services and large manufacturers dominate the index. Second, a sum hides its parts. GDP can grow at a perfectly respectable pace while consumption stalls and investment races, and those two outcomes are a different world for a fast-moving consumer goods company and a power equipment maker. Third, markets price change, not levels. A sector growing fast but slowing down often underperforms one growing slowly but speeding up.

The market does not pay for growth. It pays for growth that is accelerating faster than it expected.

So the useful habit is to break growth into its engines and ask, for each one, two questions. Is it speeding up or slowing down? And which listed sectors does it feed? Consumption feeds staples, autos, retail, consumer durables, travel and the lenders that finance them. Investment feeds capital goods, cement, steel, engineering and construction. Government spending feeds defence, railways, roads and the contractors behind them. Exports feed IT services, pharmaceuticals, chemicals and, more and more, electronics.

In a normal cycle these engines move roughly together. In this one, they have moved far apart, and that is exactly why reading them separately has paid off so well.

sections.heading: The state lit the fire
sections.html:
Go back to 2020. The pandemic had crushed demand, companies were sitting on idle capacity, and nobody was building anything. Many large companies had only just finished repairing their balance sheets after the bad-loan years of the 2010s, and they were in no mood to borrow again. Somebody had to spend.

The government chose to. From the budget of 2021 onward it raised its capital expenditure sharply, by about a third in that year alone, and kept it high. The money went into highways, railway lines and new trains, freight corridors, airports, water projects and defence equipment. This is public capex: the government building physical assets rather than paying salaries or subsidies.

The logic was a relay race. Public spending would fill the order books of engineering and construction firms, which would buy steel, cement and machinery. That would lift factory utilisation, the share of existing capacity actually in use. Once utilisation got high enough and balance sheets were strong enough, private companies would build new capacity themselves. The government would then hand over the baton.

The first leg worked well. Order books at engineering and capital goods companies swelled to record levels, cement and steel volumes rose, and the stocks of those companies were among the best performers of the post-pandemic market. Railway and defence suppliers, once sleepy public sector names, turned into retail investor favourites.

The hand-off has been the problem. Public capex can fill order books, but it cannot force a private company to build a plant. And there is a limit to how long the government can keep raising its own spending, because, as the balance sheet chapter explains, every rupee it invests has to be borrowed from the same pool of savings everyone else draws on.

sections.heading: Private capex: only where the incentives point
sections.html:
So did private investment arrive? Yes, but in a very particular pattern. It came almost entirely where the government made it worth a company's while.

The main tool was the production-linked incentive scheme, launched in 2020. The idea is simple: the government pays manufacturers a cash bonus tied to how much extra they produce in India. Electronics was the showcase. Apple's contract manufacturers set up and expanded iPhone assembly in India, and within a few years smartphones went from a minor line in the export statistics to India's single largest export category.

A few other areas saw genuine private building. Power equipment and transmission boomed, because every new solar and wind farm needs a grid to connect to. Renewables themselves attracted large corporate groups. Defence manufacturing grew as the government pushed for weapons to be made at home rather than imported.

Outside those pockets, many companies stayed cautious. Why build a new plant when existing ones are not running at full tilt and consumer demand is patchy? That is the lesson of the Goa tax cut: lower taxes raise profits immediately, but companies build only when they can see demand to fill the new capacity.

[[fig:1]]

The chart shows three slices of industrial output, each as growth over the same month a year earlier. The top panel, capital goods, is the clearest footprint of investment: it has run hottest of the three, carried by public and incentive-led building. The middle panel, consumer durables such as fridges, air conditioners and televisions, swings with festive stocking and the availability of credit. The bottom panel, manufacturing as a whole, is the average of everything. When the top panel starts to drift down while the middle one picks up, the baton is passing from investment to consumption.

sections.heading: Consumption: two Indias at the checkout
sections.html:
Consumption is the biggest engine of all, more than half of GDP. And in this cycle it has split in two. Economists call it a K-shaped recovery: one arm going up, the other going sideways or down.

The upper arm is the urban, salaried, affluent India. It has bought SUVs instead of hatchbacks, flown more than ever, filled premium hotels and bought expensive phones on easy instalments. Companies selling to that customer had a terrific few years. The lower arm is the mass and rural India. Entry-level two-wheelers and small cars struggled for a long time. Fast-moving consumer goods companies, the soap, biscuit and shampoo makers, reported sluggish volumes quarter after quarter, and much of their growth came from price increases rather than more units sold.

Why the split? Incomes at the bottom grew slowly after the pandemic, while food inflation repeatedly ate into what was left. Part of the earlier boom in mass spending was fuelled by small personal loans, and when the RBI tightened rules on unsecured lending, that tap slowed too.

Policy then leaned hard towards the lower arm. The budget of February 2025 made income up to twelve lakh rupees a year effectively tax-free under the new regime, putting money in the hands of the middle class. In September 2025 the goods and services tax was simplified into two main rates, which cut prices of everyday items, small cars, two-wheelers and appliances just before the festive season. Both were aimed squarely at mass consumption.

Here's the problem. In 2026, higher fuel prices and the RBI's turn to tightening are working against that support. A tax cut puts money in a household's pocket; a costlier fuel bill and a pricier loan take it back out. Which force wins will decide whether the lower arm finally catches up.

sections.heading: Exports: services steady, goods in a tariff storm
sections.html:
The fourth engine is the world. India earns from two kinds of exports, and they are behaving very differently.

Services are India's quiet superpower. IT services firms, consulting and back-office work, and increasingly the global capability centres that multinationals run in Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Pune, bring in a steady flow of dollars. Together with money sent home by Indians working abroad, services exports go a long way towards offsetting the oil and gold bill. They have slowed, as Western clients trimmed technology budgets, but they remain the stabiliser of the external account.

Goods exports are in a tougher spot. In August 2025 the United States raised tariffs on most Indian goods to among the highest it charges anyone, adding a penalty for India's purchases of Russian oil on top of an earlier tariff. For labour-intensive exporters selling to American buyers, such as textiles, jewellery and seafood, that is a serious blow, because their margins are thin and rivals in other countries face lower duties.

The exception is, again, electronics. Smartphones were left out of those tariffs, and India's incentive-backed assembly lines kept shipping. It is a neat illustration of the whole chapter: where policy has deliberately built capacity, the engine keeps running even in a storm.

One more warning sign. Recently imports have been growing much faster than exports, partly because oil is dearer and partly because a capex boom sucks in imported machinery and components. That widens the external gap, which is exactly the variable that makes India fragile when oil spikes.

sections.heading: How to tell which engine is accelerating
sections.html:
You do not need to wait for quarterly GDP to know which engine is speeding up. A handful of monthly indicators tell you well before.

  • For investment: capital goods output, cement and steel volumes, the order books that engineering companies report each quarter, and the government's own monthly capex spending. The RBI's survey of capacity utilisation tells you how close factories are to needing new plants.
  • For mass consumption: sales of entry-level two-wheelers and tractors, rural wage growth, and the volume growth that consumer goods companies report, not their revenue.
  • For premium consumption: SUV and luxury car sales, air passenger numbers, hotel room rates and credit card spending.
  • For exports: the monthly trade data, the order commentary from IT services companies, and electronics shipments.
  • Across the board: tax collections on goods and services, and bank credit growth broken down by who is borrowing.

The trick is to look at the direction, not the level. A number that is still high but falling is a warning. A number that is low but rising is an opportunity. Professionals call this watching the second derivative: not how fast something is growing, but whether that growth is speeding up or slowing down.

And watch the gaps between engines. When they move together, the whole index rises and falls as one. When they diverge, as now, the winners and losers inside the index can be years apart in performance. That dispersion is where stock-pickers earn their keep, and where index investors can be quietly surprised by what is carrying them.

history.title: Highways and India Shining
history.story:
In January 1999 Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee laid the foundation stone for the Golden Quadrilateral, a network of four- and six-lane highways linking Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata. Construction got going in earnest from 2001. For truckers used to crawling along potholed two-lane roads, it was a revelation, and a new generation of road contractors was born.

By 2004 the economy was humming and the ruling alliance campaigned on the slogan India Shining. It lost the election. Rural voters, it turned out, did not feel the shine.
history.lesson: Public infrastructure can kick-start a capex cycle, but headline growth can hide a mass economy that feels left out.

history.title: The IPO that rang the bell
history.story:
The mid-2000s brought India's great private capex boom. Power plants, steel mills, ports and airports were planned on a giant scale, financed by eager banks and buoyed by booming global demand. Infrastructure promoters became celebrities.

In January 2008 Anil Ambani's Reliance Power launched its IPO. Millions of retail investors applied and the issue was oversubscribed many times over, even though the company had no operating power plant. On listing day in February it opened well above its issue price, then slumped below it before the closing bell. Over the following months the global crisis deepened, and many of the boom's projects became the bad loans of the next decade.
history.lesson: Booms financed by bank debt end in bad loans, and a frenzied IPO is often the sign the cycle has peaked.

history.title: Coal, courts and stalled projects
history.story:
By the early 2010s the boom had soured into policy paralysis. Projects stalled for want of land, environmental clearances and fuel. In 2012 a scandal over how coal blocks had been handed out to companies exploded into national news, quickly nicknamed Coalgate.

In September 2014 the Supreme Court cancelled nearly every coal block allocation made since 1993, calling them illegal. Power plants that had been built around a captive coal mine suddenly had no assured fuel. Their lenders, mostly state-owned banks, were left holding loans to projects that could not pay.
history.lesson: Stalled projects do not just pause growth; they sit on bank balance sheets and choke new lending for years.

history.title: The twin balance sheet clean-up
history.story:
The chief economic adviser, Arvind Subramanian, gave the mess a name: the twin balance sheet problem. Over-borrowed companies could not invest, and the banks that had lent to them could not lend. In 2015 the RBI under Raghuram Rajan ran an asset quality review that forced banks to stop pretending and recognise their bad loans.

In 2016 India passed a bankruptcy code, and in June 2017 the RBI named a dozen giant defaulters that banks had to drag to the bankruptcy court. The press called them the dirty dozen. The biggest test, Essar Steel, ended only in November 2019, when the Supreme Court cleared ArcelorMittal's takeover.
history.lesson: Repair takes most of a decade and suppresses private capex throughout, so do not expect a new cycle until balance sheets are clean.

history.title: The Goa surprise
history.story:
With growth slowing, Nirmala Sitharaman flew to Goa ahead of a tax council meeting and announced a deep cut in the corporate tax rate, plus an even lower rate for new manufacturing companies. The Sensex closed with its biggest single-day gain in over a decade.

Profits did rise, and balance sheets got even healthier. But a broad investment wave did not follow, and within months the pandemic made the question moot.
history.lesson: Tax cuts lift profits faster than they lift capex; companies build when they see demand, not just when they keep more of their earnings.

history.title: The state steps in, and the iPhone arrives
history.story:
In April 2020, in the depths of the lockdown, the government launched its production-linked incentive scheme for mobile phones, and later extended the idea to other sectors. Apple's Taiwanese contract manufacturers, led by Foxconn's plant in Tamil Nadu, scaled up iPhone assembly. A decade earlier smartphones barely figured in India's export list. By FY25 they were its single largest export category.

Meanwhile the budget of 2021 raised public capex by about a third and kept raising it. Roads, railways and defence orders filled order books, and capital goods stocks became the market's darlings.
history.lesson: Public capex and targeted incentives can fill order books, but they cannot force private capex outside the sectors they pay for.

history.title: The turn to the consumer
history.story:
By 2025 the government's attention had shifted to the struggling mass consumer. The February budget made income up to twelve lakh rupees a year effectively tax-free under the new regime. In September the goods and services tax was collapsed into two main rates from the first day of Navratri, and buyers queued for newly cheaper small cars. Maruti Suzuki said it was on course for the busiest single day of deliveries in its history.

Then 2026 brought the Iran war, a surge in oil prices and an RBI forced to raise rates to defend the rupee. The support for the mass consumer now has to fight a costlier fuel bill and dearer loans.
history.lesson: Policy can tilt which engine accelerates, but an oil shock can claw back a tax cut within months.

What to watch next: whether capital goods growth keeps slowing in the next few prints, how festive-season volumes compare with last year for two-wheelers and entry cars, and whether the gap between import and export growth narrows.
sowhat:
The capex complex still has momentum but is decelerating from a very high pace, and consumption faces an income squeeze from fuel and rates. Expect dispersion inside the index to widen.

  • Prefer the incentive-backed pockets of investment where order books are long and demand is policy-driven: power equipment and transmission, electronics manufacturing and defence. Their visibility is better than the broad capex trade.
  • Be careful with capex names priced for acceleration. When growth decelerates from a very high pace, stocks priced for perfection tend to de-rate even as profits keep growing.
  • Be careful with mass consumption: entry-level autos and staples face a fuel and rates squeeze that can offset the tax cuts.
  • Premium consumption has been resilient, but it leans on wealth effects from the stock market and property, so it is not immune to a drawdown.
  • Export-oriented goods makers selling to American buyers carry tariff risk; services exporters are steadier but slower.

What would flip it: oil falling back and the RBI easing would release the mass consumer, letting the tax and GST cuts finally show up in volumes. A sustained rebound in capital goods growth, or clear signs of private capex spreading beyond incentive sectors, would extend the investment trade.
